model.author: Bio3D Project
model.modifications: Procedural 3D bony fish anatomy model exported as GLB.

short.en: A smooth, boat-shaped body covered in slippery scales to glide easily through water.

detail.en: Fusiform (streamlined) body covered with overlapping dermal scales (cycloid or ctenoid in bony fish) and mucus to reduce drag in water.

short.en: Front end of the fish used for eating food and taking in water for breathing.

detail.en: Bony fishes (Osteichthyes) typically have a terminal mouth; water enters through the mouth and is pumped across the gills.

short.en: Large lidless eyes on each side of the head for spotting food and predators underwater.

detail.en: Fish eyes have spherical lenses adapted for underwater vision and lack eyelids (staying moist naturally in water).

short.en: A protective bony flap covering the gills; opens and closes to pump water over them.

detail.en: Present in bony fishes (Osteichthyes) and absent in cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes like sharks). Shields delicate gill filaments and pumps water continuously.

short.en: The top fin that acts like a ship's keel to keep the fish upright and balanced.

detail.en: Unpaired median fin on the dorsal surface preventing rolling so the fish stays steady while swimming or turning.

short.en: A pair of side fins near the head used for steering, hovering, and braking.

detail.en: Paired anterior fins corresponding to the forelimbs of land vertebrates. Provide fine manoeuvrability, turning, and stopping.

short.en: Bottom fins that help keep the fish level and stop it from tipping sideways.

detail.en: Paired pelvic fins (ventral) and unpaired anal fin (posterior ventral) work together with the dorsal fin to stabilise pitch and roll.

short.en: The powerful back fin that sweeps side-to-side to push the fish forward.

detail.en: Homocercal (symmetrical lobes) in most bony fishes; generates forward thrust and acts as a rudder for sharp direction changes.

short.en: Feathery red breathing organs under the gill cover that absorb dissolved oxygen from water.

detail.en: Four pairs of filamentous gill arches in Osteichthyes. Rich capillary beds use counter-current exchange — blood flows opposite to water — maximising O₂ uptake.

short.en: An internal gas-filled sac that lets bony fish float effortlessly without sinking.

detail.en: Hydrostatic organ regulating buoyancy in Osteichthyes (absent in Chondrichthyes like sharks, which must swim continuously or rely on oily livers).

short.en: A line of tiny sensors along each side that detects water vibrations and nearby movement.

detail.en: Mechanoreceptive canal running along the flanks containing neuromast hair cells. Detects pressure changes, currents, prey, and obstacles even in murky water.

question.en: Tap the powerful back fin that pushes the fish forward through the water.

explanation.en: The tail (caudal) fin sweeps side-to-side to create forward thrust and helps steer the fish.

question.en: Which part protects the delicate gills and helps pump water over them?

explanation.en: The operculum is a bony flap on each side of a bony fish's head that covers the gills and pumps water past them.

question.en: Tap the internal organ that controls buoyancy in bony fishes (Osteichthyes).

explanation.en: The swim bladder adjusts gas volume so bony fish can stay neutrally buoyant at different depths without sinking.

question.en: Which sensory system runs along the sides of a fish to detect water vibrations?

explanation.en: The lateral line contains neuromast receptors that sense vibrations and pressure waves in the surrounding water.
